//: e0: restitution at low impact speed; eSlope: loss per m/s of normal speed; eMin floor. mu: sliding friction, as measured at light impacts; muFall: how fast it falls per m/s of normal speed above muRef, mu / (1 + muFall * (speed - muRef)). muRef 8.5 m/s is the hardest impact the published numbers reach: the ITF court pace test (30 m/s at 16 deg, 8.3 m/s) and Cross's change from sliding to gripping (20 m/s at 25 deg, 8.5 m/s). Felt grips less the harder it is pressed (Hertzian contact: friction ~ load^-1/3). No padel measurement exists: floors' 0.12 and glass's 0.35 are fitted to how pros' smashes end (W 45; winners double bounce 48, came back over the net 35, out 17; these give W 53, winners 53/37/7), and with mu held flat a rolling ball climbed the back glass to 4.8 m at the median and 65% of smashes flew back over the net unplayed. Glass at 0.12 still took a smash that met it at 1.1 m up to 3.9 m. grip: how much contact-point velocity reverses when the ball grips (0 = rolls out, 0.3 = lively). jitterDeg: random tilt of the normal (never more than half the angle the ball comes in at, so a glancing hit can't turn into a second contact); turnDeg: random sideways turn of the rebound about the surface normal (the sand's scatter on a floor: it skews the ball without changing how high it bounces); speedJitter: random fraction of rebound speed lost. Sources (docs/realism.md, Phase 1 in DECISIONS.md): the slope of restitution with impact speed is the ball's own (pressurised tennis balls on a rigid surface fall from about 0.80 at 3 m/s to 0.60 at 20 m/s, Dignall 2004), so every hard surface uses about 0.0115 per m/s and e0 is set so the FIP drop test (2.54 m, about 6.9 m/s) bounces 141 cm on hard. turf: sand-filled turf is almost a rigid floor for a ball (tennis: 100.7% of concrete's drop rebound, Hamilton 2000; padel standard UNE 41958 IN asks >= 80%), and padel balls on a padel court show friction 0.56-0.62 (IBV for Testfakta 2023, 10 balls, 70 km/h; the angle isn't published, the lab assumes the ITF's 16 deg); the sand's scatter is tuning (no data): mostly sideways (turnDeg 2), height within a few per cent (jitter 0.3, speedJitter 0.03), so bounce height is as true as on hard while the line of the ball wanders a degree or two. glass: tempered 10-12 mm panels are near-rigid walls (plate impedance: 1-2% of the ball's energy, so x0.985 of the rigid restitution, derived) and felt on smooth glazed tile slides at mu 0.35 (ITF test, Dignall). glassJoin: FIP wants panel joins flush and the rebound uniform, so a join is nearly a plain bounce (tuning). seam: frames (mesh posts, the mesh panel's frame along the glass top, door edges): irregular (tuning; no data). mesh: no published rebound data at all; 50 x 50 mm welded mesh, 2-4 mm wire, horizontal wires inside (FIP), about 4 kg/m2 against 30 for glass; FIP and the CSD's NIDE sheet call its rebound irregular (tuning). clay: mu from tennis clay (Cross 2010: 0.70 at 26 m/s, 17 deg); padel isn't played on clay (fantasy). rollDecel (floors): how fast a rolling ball slows, m/s per second; 0.8 on every floor until measured (no padel or tennis figure found; a ramp-roll test settles it: decel = v^2 / 2d for the distance d rolled off a ramp).

netGive.//: The net body is a tensioned mesh that gives: the ball pushes it back like a damped spring. omega: natural frequency (rad/s) in the middle of the net at mid-height, rising towards the posts, the tape and the floor as 1/sqrt(give), give = (1 - (x/halfW)^2) * 4u(1-u) with u = height / net height, floored at minGive. zeta: damping ratio (0.55 sends back about 12% of the speed). grab: how fast the mesh stops the ball sliding along it and its spin (1/s). spread: random variation of omega and zeta per catch.

netCloth.//: The net as cloth (src/sim/court/netCloth.ts). FIP: 10 m long, 0.88 m at the centre and 0.92 m at the ends, steel cable up to 1 cm inside a white tape 5-6.3 cm. Real nets: 3 mm polypropylene/polyethylene twine in 45 mm squares (about 220 g/m2, so about 2 kg of netting), 5 mm PVC-coated steel cable; with the netting hanging on it the cable sags 4 cm at about 1 kN. Twine EA about 7 kN; one link spans 1.5 cords. The bottom edge is a cord in a PVC binding laced to the posts at the floor (about 60 g/m with the binding). cordCd/solidity give the twine's air drag (solidity 2 x 3 mm / 45 mm). damping is knot friction. Contact: the netting grips (friction) and gives almost nothing back; the tape band kicks a little more; the cable more again. Substeps keep the ball under maxTravel per substep.

//junction: A ball reaching a second surface (floor and wall, or two walls in a corner) while still in contact with the first is squeezed by both at once: the two bounces are solved together, averaged over which came first (weight 1 when both are touched together, 0 once the second is a contact time away), with extra loss in the nick. contactTime: a pressurised ball's contact on a rigid surface lasts about 4 ms (tennis balls: 4-5 ms, Brody/Cross/Lindsey 2002); gap: within 1 cm (about the ball's compression at rally speeds) it touches both; loss: restitution lost at an exact nick (tuning: squash's nick is dead, a padel ball in the rincón comes out low; no measured number); nickGap: closer than this to the floor, a wall-then-floor contact counts as landing first (FIP: a ball in the corner where wall meets floor is good).
